title: What seeding can and can’t do
teaches: How little water a cloud holds at any moment, which clouds seeding can work on, where it has worked, and how to tell a real effect from a lucky winter

blocks.title: The big ideas of this lesson
points: Seeding cannot make a cloud, or make water. It can only give ice to a cloud that already holds supercooled water.
A cloud holds very little water at any moment. Storms rain for hours because they keep lifting new air and making new cloud.
Seeding works only in a window: clouds between about −5 °C and −25 °C with little natural ice of their own.
It clears supercooled fog reliably, and adds a little snow to winter clouds over mountains. Elsewhere, its effects are small or unproven.
Storms vary so much by themselves that only a fair trial, with the storms to seed picked by chance, over many winters, can show whether seeding did anything.

blocks.text: The last lesson showed seeding at its most impressive: a cloud that turns to snow minutes after a pass with dry ice. This lesson is about its limits, which matter just as much to anyone deciding whether to pay for it.
The first limit is the simplest. Seeding does not make clouds, and it does not make water. It only gives ice to a cloud that already holds supercooled water. No cloud, nothing to seed.

In a drought, the sky is usually clear for a reason. A high sits over the region and its air sinks, warming and drying as it is squeezed, as in Lesson 3. To make a cloud, air has to be lifted and cooled to its dew point, as in Lessons 1 and 2, and no amount of dry ice can lift the air over a whole county.

The second limit is how little water a cloud holds. A layer of cloud carries about 0.2 grams of liquid water in each cubic metre. Stack a kilometre of it over a square metre of ground and you have 200 grams of water. If every drop fell, it would cover the ground 0.2 millimetres deep: about the thickness of two sheets of paper.

blocks.caption: Water on the ground, from a cloud, a storm and a year.

blocks.text: How, then, does a storm drop ten or fifteen millimetres in a day? Because a cloud is not a full bucket that empties once. It is more like the spray over a waterfall: always being made afresh, as the storm lifts new moist air off the Pacific, cools it, condenses it and rains it out, hour after hour.
Seeding can only help a cloud let go of more of the water passing through it while it is there. Most of the water comes from the wind, not from the cloud overhead at any one moment.

The third limit is temperature. Seeding needs supercooled water, so it does nothing for a cloud warmer than 0 °C. Between 0 and −5 °C, only dry ice works. Between about −5 and −25 °C, dry ice and silver iodide both work, and this is where seeding has the most to offer.

Colder than about −25 °C, nature’s own ice-starting specks, which grow tenfold in number for every 4 °C colder, are already plentiful enough to freeze the cloud without help. Below −38 °C the cloud is all ice anyway, like cirrus. Adding ice to a cloud that already has plenty does nothing useful.

blocks.caption: Which clouds seeding can help, by temperature.

blocks.text: Summer cumulus over the basin is usually warm all the way through, so there is nothing to seed. By the time a heap grows far above the freezing level, it is a thunderstorm already full of its own ice, and seeding it can make it grow a little faster (freezing releases heat, like condensation in Lesson 2) or do nothing at all; experiments have never settled which.
The best candidates are the cold clouds of winter: the supercooled fog and stratus that pools in the basin under an inversion, and the clouds that winter storms pile up over the mountains.

**Supercooled fog** is seeding’s one sure success. Dry ice dropped from an aeroplane, or propane gas sprayed so that it expands and chills the air below −40 °C, fills a fog bank with crystals. They grow, fall as a light snow, and open a clear hole over a runway for an hour or so. It works every time, but only in supercooled fog; fog warmer than 0 °C does not respond at all.

**Winter clouds over mountains** are the other good case. Moist air forced up the western slopes makes supercooled cloud, and much of it crosses the crest before its water has turned to snow, then evaporates down the far side, as in the rain shadow of Lesson 7.

Silver iodide from burners on the ground, or from aircraft, can turn some of that passing water into snow on the slopes. Careful experiments have measured gains from a few percent up to perhaps fifteen percent, in the right storms. For dry country downstream, that matters: mountain snow is the river water of summer.

**Hailstorms and hurricanes** have been seeded too, in the hope of making many small hailstones instead of a few large ones, or of weakening a hurricane’s winds. Neither has ever been clearly shown to work. Storms that big have so much energy and so much natural ice that a seeder’s contribution is lost in them.
The hardest question in cloud seeding is whether it did anything. A seeder seeds a cloud, and it snows. Would it have snowed anyway?

Storms vary enormously by themselves. One winter storm over the mountains may drop three times the snow of the next for reasons that have nothing to do with seeding. An effect of ten or fifteen percent is a whisper next to that noise.

The only fair test is the one doctors use for a new medicine. Decide which storms to seed by chance, with a coin toss, before anyone knows how each will turn out. Then compare many seeded storms with many that were not. Luck evens out only when there are a great many storms on each side.

blocks.caption: A seeding trial over the mountains: each dot is one storm’s snow.
blocks.task: Run winters until the difference stands out from luck.

blocks.text: Notice two things in the figure. In the first winter or two, seeding can look as if it doubled the snow, or as if it made things worse: that is luck, not seeding. And when the seeder picks the storms, the numbers look wonderful and mean almost nothing, because a good forecaster picks the storms that were going to snow anyway.
Many of the rainmakers who travelled the West offering to end droughts made exactly that mistake, or took advantage of it. They seeded when rain looked likely, and took the credit when it came.

A second check is to compare the seeded area with a **control** area nearby that was not seeded but gets the same storms. Weather that hits both cancels out, and what is left is more likely to be the seeding.

So when someone asks a seeder to make it rain, the honest answer has a few parts. Nobody can make clouds. Sometimes you can help a supercooled cloud let go of water it would otherwise have carried away. In the right clouds, expect a small gain; in the wrong ones, nothing. And be ready to show how you know.

Every lesson in this workbook comes into that answer: what a cloud is made of, how air is lifted to make one, which floor it lives on and how cold it is there, how ice makes rain, and what kind of storm it belongs to.

blocks.title: Before you seed, ask
points: Is there a cloud? Seeding cannot make one.
Is it supercooled, between about −5 and −25 °C? Warmer, use dry ice or nothing; colder, it has its own ice.
Is it deep enough, and the air below it moist enough, for snow to reach the ground?
How much will you use? Too much overseeds.
How will you know it worked? Seed by chance, compare with storms left alone, and count many winters.

blocks.text: Seeding needs supercooled cloud, and how cold a cloud is depends on how high it is. First, call the floor of each cloud in the photos. Then answer what seeding can and can’t do for each sky.

blocks.caption: Real photos. Which floor is each cloud on?
A sky, and a question about seeding it.

items.question: A fog over the river at +3 °C keeps the ferry tied up. Will dry ice clear it?
options: No: it is warmer than 0 °C, so there is nothing to freeze
Yes: dry ice clears any fog
items.why: Seeding clears supercooled fog. Fog warmer than freezing has nothing for ice to grow from, and any crystals the dry ice makes simply melt.

items.question: A seeder picked five storms to seed last winter, and they snowed 40 percent more than the average storm. Does that prove seeding works?
options: No: he picked them, and five is far too few to beat luck
Yes: 40 percent is a big difference
Yes, if the storms were in winter
items.why: A seeder with a good eye picks the storms that were going to snow anyway, and five storms vary far more than seeding could. Only storms picked by chance, over many winters, can show a real effect.

items.question: High cirrus at −45 °C drifts over all afternoon. Would seeding it bring snow?
options: No: it is ice already, with no supercooled water to work on
Yes: it is the coldest cloud, so it seeds best
items.why: Below −38 °C every droplet freezes on its own. Cirrus is all ice already; adding more ice gives it nothing new to do.

items.question: No rain in six weeks, a few flat little heaps at noon that never grow, and the barometer high and steady. A man from California wants two thousand dollars to make it rain. Should the Grange hire him?
options: No: a high is keeping the air sinking, and there is no supercooled cloud to seed
Yes: seeding works on any cloud
items.why: Under a high, sinking air keeps the heaps small, flat and warm. Seeding cannot lift air or make cloud; it can only give ice to supercooled water, and there is none here.

items.question: The doctor from Spokane can’t land for the fog. It’s −7 °C and there’s rime on everything. Can anything be done?
options: Yes: seed the supercooled fog over the runway with dry ice to open a hole for an hour or so
No: fog can never be cleared
Wait for a thunderstorm to blow it away
items.why: Rime means the fog is supercooled. Dry ice fills it with crystals that grow and fall as a light snow, clearing a hole over the runway long enough to land.

items.question: If somebody seeds that big thunderstorm building over the hills, will it rain on my wheat instead of passing by?
options: Not reliably: a thunderstorm is full of its own ice, and seeding’s effect on it is unproven
Yes: seeded storms always rain where they are seeded
Yes, and it will stop the hail too
items.why: By the time a heap is a thunderstorm, it is far into the ice realm and full of natural ice. Seeding storms that big has never been shown to change where or how much they rain.

learned: Seeding cannot make clouds or water: it only gives ice to a cloud that already holds supercooled water, so clear skies under a high, as in a drought, have nothing to seed.
A cloud layer a kilometre deep holds only about 0.2 mm of water; storms rain for hours because they keep lifting new moist air and making new cloud.
Seeding works in a window, roughly −5 to −25 °C: warmer clouds have nothing to freeze (or need dry ice), colder ones have plenty of natural ice, and below −38 °C they are all ice.

Seeding reliably clears supercooled fog, and adds a few percent, perhaps up to fifteen, to the snow of winter clouds over mountains; for hailstorms and hurricanes, it has never been clearly shown to work.

Storms vary so much by themselves that only a fair trial, with the storms to seed picked by chance, compared over many winters and with an unseeded control area, can show whether seeding did anything.

cloud-water.title: How much water a cloud holds
cloud-water.text: About 0.2 grams of liquid water in each cubic metre of a layer cloud: a kilometre of it, wrung out completely, would wet the ground 0.2 mm deep. A storm drops 10 to 15 mm in a day only because it keeps lifting new moist air and making new cloud for hours. Seeding cannot make cloud or water; it can only help a cloud let go of what passes through it.

seeding-window.title: The seeding window
seeding-window.text: Seeding needs supercooled water and a shortage of natural ice. Above 0 °C there is nothing to freeze; from 0 to −5 °C only dry ice works; from about −5 to −25 °C dry ice and silver iodide both work; colder, natural specks make enough ice already, and below −38 °C clouds are all ice.

seeding-works.title: Where seeding works
seeding-works.text: It clears supercooled fog every time, opening a hole over a runway for an hour or so. Over mountains in winter, silver iodide can turn some of the supercooled cloud that would have crossed the crest into snow on the slopes: careful experiments find a few percent to perhaps fifteen percent more, in the right storms. For hail and hurricanes, no clear effect has ever been shown.

fair-trial.title: A fair trial
fair-trial.text: Storms vary so much by themselves that one winter, or a seeder’s own pick of storms, proves nothing. Pick the storms to seed by chance, compare many seeded storms with many left alone, over many winters, and compare the seeded area with an unseeded control area nearby. A real effect of ten or fifteen percent takes hundreds of storms to see.
